p: Brigadier General James J. Archer was trying to cross the run when Private Patrick Maloney of the 2nd Wisconsin grabbed him by the collar.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Archer was a small, sick man — he had been ill for weeks and had no business commanding a brigade in the field. He looked up at the private holding him and said simply that he would not be taken.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Archer was brought to Doubleday, who had just assumed command after Reynolds's death. The two men knew each other from before the war. Doubleday extended his hand and said cheerfully, 'Good morning, Archer! How are you? I am glad to see you!'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Archer refused to shake hands. 'Well, I am not glad to see YOU by a damn sight, Doubleday.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He was the first Confederate general officer captured since Lee had taken command of the Army of Northern Virginia. He would spend the rest of the campaign in a Union prison.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Rufus Dawes had been a schoolteacher before the war. On the morning of July 1, 1863, he was commanding the 6th Wisconsin — the largest regiment in the Iron Brigade — and watching Davis's Confederate brigade sweep north past his position toward the unfinished railroad cut.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 1 of 10

p: Dawes received orders to charge. He turned to his men.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 2 of 10

p: 'Six Wisconsin, advance!' The regiment stepped off at the double-quick, moving north across the Chambersburg Pike. The 14th Brooklyn — red-legged Zouaves — joined on their left. The 95th New York came with them.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 3 of 10

p: Davis's men had ducked into the railroad cut for cover. It seemed perfect — a ready-made trench running east-west. What Davis had not understood was that the western portion of the cut was fifteen feet deep. His men were trapped in a ditch.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 4 of 10

p: Dawes's regiment hit the cut at a run. The fighting was vicious — men stabbed each other with bayonets across a gap of feet, grappled over regimental flags, fired at point-blank range. But the Confederates could not climb the sheer walls under fire.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 5 of 10

p: Dawes reached the middle of the cut and shouted across to the Confederate officer opposite him: 'Where is the colonel of this regiment?'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 6 of 10

p: 'Who are you?' the officer called back.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 7 of 10

p: 'I am Colonel Dawes of the 6th Wisconsin. I demand the immediate and unconditional surrender of this regiment!'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 8 of 10

p: There was a pause. Then the Confederate flag dipped, and men began throwing down their arms.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The Railroad Cut”, paragraph 9 of 10

p: Dawes captured 232 prisoners — nearly a full regiment — in a single charge. The regimental flag of the 2nd Mississippi was taken. Davis's brigade had been broken for the second time in a morning.
